Combat Robots

Subteam Leader and Mechanical Engineer, Rice Robotics Club · Onshape, 3D printing, waterjet, machining, soldering

A series of plastic antweight combat robots. Each new bot fixes the problems found in the previous one. I lead twice-weekly build sessions for 15 members, and I co-organized Rice's combat robotics competition, which drew 50+ competitors, coordinating vendors, securing sponsors, and managing event logistics. My first full-combat antweight, Archer, follows in DWG 002.

Rev A

Sparky

Plastic antweight · Vertical spinner · Fall 2025

My first bot. It competed at a regional competition in Houston and lost badly, and nearly every subsystem needed rework. These are the changes I carried into the next builds:

Changes for the next build
  • Weapon: make it larger, open the shaft bore by 0.100" for clearance, add a weapon key, blunt the striking edge (too sharp and it chips instead of biting), reinforce the base, and use a 0.75" striking face
  • Balance: fix the 0.400" counterweight spacing and move the center of mass
  • Chassis: thicker base plate, fillets where wires pass through, and wheel covers
  • Wedge: make it smaller with a slight curve
  • Drive: add a rear skid so the front does not lift when accelerating, and move to 2.5" wheels

Rev B

Goblin

Plastic antweight · Vertical spinner · Spring 2026

The second bot, built from Sparky's change list. I made the weapon bigger and the chassis compact, with less internal space so components would not shift around while driving, which was a problem on Sparky. Goblin competed at the Dallas competition. The compact layout went too far, though. It was so tight that fitting and servicing components at competitions was difficult.

Changes for the next build
  • Layout: make more internal space available. Components were too cramped to service
  • Balance: keep the weight low in the chassis for a stable orientation
  • Weapon: stronger support, and consider supporting the weapon on both sides
  • Driving: make the bot able to drive upside down
Fig. 5: CAD model
Fig. 6: Assembled bot
Rev C

Barbarian

Plastic antweight · Vertical spinner · Spring 2026

My most recent bot, built after applying the changes from Sparky and Goblin. The chassis is flat, which gives it better balance and enough room to fit every component comfortably, unlike Goblin. I also added wedges at the front for combat. It competed at the Rice battle bots competition and fought better than the earlier bots, winning a match. It could still drive after being flipped upside down, but in that position it was very vulnerable to attack, and it lost to a horizontal spinner. It still placed second overall at the competition.

Changes for the next build
  • Body: build a more resistant structure. The bot is exposed to attack when it is upside down
  • Armor: better protection against horizontal spinners

Dwg No.002
ClassFull-combat antweight
MaterialsUHMW · TPU · PLA · Carbon steel
DateFall 2026

Archer

Full-combat antweight · Vertical spinner · Designed in Autodesk Fusion · CNC-machined

My first full-combat antweight, and a big step up from the plastic bots. This is where I learned material selection, CNC machining, and tolerancing, instead of just printing everything in PLA.

Material selection
UHMW Rail. Tough and slippery. It takes hits and dents instead of cracking, and the low-friction surface makes spinners skid off instead of digging in
TPU Body. Flexible, so it bends and soaks up a hit instead of cracking like a stiff plastic would
PLA Covers. They take hits, but they are easy to replace. PLA is stiff so the cover holds its shape instead of bending inward like TPU would, and it is cheap and fast to reprint, so I just print a new one when it breaks
Carbon steel Weapon disk and front forks. These need real metal strength to take and deliver spinner hits. The printed plastics would not survive where the weapon makes contact
Machining

I CNC-machined the UHMW rail. It needed M3 holes drilled into the side, which is tough to line up by hand on a slippery material, so I made a jig to hold the rail and keep each hole straight.

What I'd improve

The back was the weak spot. It was only covered in TPU, and I ran the wires through a pocket there, so a hit from behind could get to them. Next time the rear needs more protection and the wiring needs to run somewhere safer.

Split-Hopkinson Bar Safety Cage

Undergraduate Research Assistant · Rice, Prof. Matthew Brake · SolidWorks · T-slot + acrylic

Our lab uses a mini split-Hopkinson pressure bar to study how energy moves across bolted joints under a shock load. I designed and built the safety enclosure around it: a T-slot frame with clear acrylic panels that contains the bar if something lets go, while staying see-through for the high-speed cameras and DIC.

Design notes
  • Switched the lid from a hinge-and-latch design to panels that slide into the T-slot, after thinking through how the old design could fail during a containment event
  • The cage is stable as built. The one thing left is that the top lids can slide, so we are adding velcro to hold them in place during a test
Build challenge

The lab's waterjet was down, so I could not cut the acrylic the easy way. I cut all the panels by hand on a powered saw instead, which made clean, square edges a lot harder to get.

Still to come

More of the rig is still being built. Next up are a smaller cage and the bars themselves, and I will add them here as they come together.
